title: Crumbs and Ephphatha (Mark 7:24–37)
hookLine: a foreign mother wins an argument with Jesus, and a deaf man hears be opened

cards: Jesus walks north, out of Galilee, into the country around Tyre, on the coast. Foreign land. Mark says he went into a house and wanted nobody to know he was there.
It doesn't work. A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish; Mark calls her a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth.
Her little daughter is tormented by an unclean spirit, and she falls at his feet and begs. What he says back is hard to hear. What she says back to him is quick.
Then, on the way home, a man who can't hear.

teach.h: THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.
teach.b: First, the hard line. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Suffer first the children to be filled: for it is not good to take the bread of the children, and cast it to the dogs."
Readers take the children as Israel and the dogs as everyone else. It stings. Some hear a test of her faith; some simply let it be hard.
Mark doesn't explain. Second, her answer. She doesn't leave.

teach.h: EVEN THE WHELPS EAT THE CRUMBS.
teach.b: She takes his own picture and turns it: "Yea, Lord; for the whelps also eat under the table of the crumbs of the children." Whelps: young dogs, the ones under the table. Fine, she says, I'm under the table.
Crumbs fall. And he gives way: "For this saying go thy way," and her daughter is healed. It's her words, this saying, that he points to.
Third, the deaf man. Back near the Sea of Galilee, people bring a man who is deaf and can hardly speak.

teach.h: FINGERS, SPIT, A GROAN, A WORD.
teach.b: Jesus takes him aside, away from the crowd, puts his fingers in the man's ears, spits and touches his tongue. He looks up to heaven, groans, and says one word in Aramaic: "Ephpheta, which is, Be thou opened."
Mark kept the sound. Fourth, where the word lives now.
At a Catholic baptism, the priest may touch the child's ears and mouth and pray that they be opened, to hear the word and proclaim the faith.
It's called the Ephphetha rite. A groan by a lake became part of how the Church welcomes a baby.

how: In the Catholic rite of baptism for children, the priest may touch the child's ears and mouth and pray that the child soon hear the word and proclaim the faith, a gesture called the Ephphetha, taken from Mark 7.

o: be opened: the word spoken to a deaf man
be healed: a blessing said over the sick
be quiet: Jesus calming a noisy crowd

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're the mother. you've begged for your daughter, and he says it isn't good to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. what do you do?
o: answer that even the dogs eat the crumbs under the table.
argue that you deserve it more than anyone.
games.why: "Yea, Lord; for the whelps also eat under the table of the crumbs of the children." and he answers, for this saying, go thy way.

practice: Touch your ears lightly with your fingertips, then your lips, and name one place you've gone closed: a person you stopped listening to, a word you keep swallowing, a door you locked a while ago.
If you pray, say the one word Jesus said: be opened. If you don't, let your hands rest open on your knees, and breathe toward that closed place.

wordCard.voice: Ephphatha. Aramaic: be opened. Spoken to a deaf man by the Sea of Galilee, and still spoken at baptisms. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters by Mark: be opened.

carryVoice: Your line: be opened. The mother made him listen all the way to the end. That's day two hundred eleven.
